newsitem.title: GERMANY: German Stasi informants win some legal protection.
newsitem.headline: German Stasi informants win some legal protection.

text.p: Germany on Friday gave some protection to ex-informants for former East Germany's Stasi secret police, deciding employers had no right to know of their spying if it took place before 1976.
The law, passed by the Bonn parliament, acknowledged many of the estimated 175,000 unofficial spies were small fry or worked only briefly for the feared Ministry for State Security (Stasi).
United Germany has screened east Germans to stop informers and employees of the Stasi getting jobs as civil servants, teachers or police.
Employers were entitled to get information from the "Gauck authority" which controls access to the files.
But many affected employees have won court appeals forcing employers to take or keep them on despite their Stasi past.
Peter Busse, director of the Gauck authority, told German Radio the reform, six years after German unification, would "give some former Stasi informers the chance to take a place in society again".
But he rejected the fears of many former east German dissidents and civil rights activists that it marked the first step towards a general amnesty for Stasi workers.

"An important aspect is that victims can still get to see their files and so still find out about and deal with activities that took place before the cut-off date. So can media and researchers," Busse said.
"We are not locking away a part of the files, simply limiting employers' rights to request information."
The volume of information accumulated by the Stasi, which had 90,000 full-time workers in addition to a network of neighbourhood and workplace spies, runs to 180 km (112 miles) of shelf-space.

The demand for information from those who suffered at the Stasi's hands is unabated. When Bonn politicians made an abortive attempt in 1994 to limit victims' access to the Stasi files, the number of applications to see them tripled.
Now 15,000 such requests are filed with the Gauck authority each month.
There are signs employers are more ready to turn a blind eye to former Stasi involvement, particularly when the alternative is to gut large parts of east German public institutions.
"Around five percent of Berlin's schoolteachers were found to have informed for the Stasi, but only about one in four with confirmed Stasi ties lost their jobs."
In the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, two-thirds of the public servants exposed as Stasi informers still have jobs.
